claims.statement: Numerical systems provide the strongest material continuity between pre-writing devices and proto-cuneiform.
claims.counterevidence: Continuity of individual non-numerical sign shapes is much less secure.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: Neolithic clay objects called tokens were multifunctional; their existence does not prove a millennia-long standardized accounting code.
claims.counterevidence: Some late simple tokens in bullae clearly served numerical/accounting functions.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: The direct token→tablet→writing sequence is too linear; seals, iconography, bullae, numerical tablets and institutional practice formed a parallel ecology.
claims.counterevidence: Exact contribution of each component cannot be quantified.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: Administrative scale is a major formation pressure but not evidence that administration was the sole cause of writing.
claims.counterevidence: Preserved earliest texts are overwhelmingly administrative, but corpus survival is selective.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: The evidence supports a feedback model: expanding institutions demanded records, and better records could expand institutional capacity.
claims.counterevidence: Downstream effects require WS06 case studies; WS02 cannot establish them alone.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: The preserved proto-cuneiform corpus can distinguish accounting contexts more securely than it can distinguish market exchange from tax, tribute or redistribution.
claims.counterevidence: Named agents, commodities, metrology and document structure sometimes narrow the transaction, but sign readings and institutional context remain incomplete.
claims.narrative_implication: Use 'accounting/administrative transfer' unless reciprocity or institutional flow is independently demonstrated.

claims.statement: Redistribution, labor coordination, obligation and ownership are not interchangeable formation mechanisms: each requires different evidence beyond the presence of numbers and commodities.
claims.counterevidence: A single tablet may participate in more than one mechanism, and early terminology is partly reconstructed.
claims.narrative_implication: Label the mechanism only when flows, persons, quotas, duration, seals or transfer conditions support it.

claims.statement: Co-occurrence between urban institutional growth and record systems establishes pressure and compatibility, not a one-way proof that either caused the other.
claims.counterevidence: Later cases may demonstrate capacity effects, but those belong to WS06 and cannot be back-projected.
claims.narrative_implication: Present the WS02 feedback loop as a hypothesis to be tested, not as a completed causal verdict.

sources.title: Proto-Cuneiform Account-Books and Journals
sources.author: Robert K. Englund
sources.authority: Leading specialist synthesis grounded in the archaic tablet corpus and CDLI work.
locators: pp. 24–27 (PDF pp. 2–5), especially chronology figure and discussion of Uruk IV/III corpus
limitations: Chronological ranges and corpus counts reflect the state of publication in 2004; some causal interpretation belongs to WS02.
Older chronology; causal interpretation remains debated.
notes: Supports ca. 3300 BCE emergence, relative Uruk IV→III sequence, overwhelmingly administrative earliest corpus, and caution around token continuity.
Selected for this workstream's bounded question.

sources.title: Writing in Early Mesopotamia: Beyond the Meme
sources.author: Massimo Maiocchi
sources.authority: Assyriological synthesis focused on early Mesopotamian writing, semiotics and material systems.
locators: pp. 410–412 (PDF pp. 15–17), especially discussion of glottographic/semasiographic boundary
limitations: The chapter advocates a fluid continuum; terminology is analytical rather than a universally accepted threshold definition.
Framework-oriented rather than a new excavation report.
notes: Useful counterweight to a binary true-writing/proto-writing distinction and to a linear token→tablet story.
Selected for this workstream's bounded question.

sources.title: Visible Language: Inventions of Writing in the Ancient Middle East and Beyond
sources.author: Christopher Woods (ed.)
sources.authority: University of Chicago Oriental Institute catalogue curated by a Sumerologist.
locators: comparative chronology and essays on earliest Mesopotamian and Egyptian writing; catalogue overview
limitations: Catalogue compresses specialist disagreements for comparative presentation; use for comparison scope, not exact Uruk stratigraphy.
Comparative overview; some pathways remain hypothetical.
notes: Treats Mesopotamia and Egypt as roughly contemporary independent inventions; supports avoiding an unqualified unique 'world first' claim.
Selected for this workstream's bounded question.

sources.title: Reconsidering ‘Tokens’
sources.author: Lucy E. Bennison-Chapman, 2019
limitations: Full text access limited; abstract supports multifunctionality critique.
notes: Selected for this workstream's bounded question.

sources.title: A Quantitative Analysis of Proto-Cuneiform Sign Use in Archaic Tribute
sources.author: Logan Born and Kathryn Erin Kelley, 2021
locators: §§1–3; corpus definition, sign-frequency and genre limits
limitations: Sign-frequency patterns do not by themselves establish sign meanings or causal direction.
Readability, sign variants, genre assignment and corpus growth constrain quantitative conclusions.
notes: Used to test how far administrative subgenres can be distinguished from the preserved corpus.
Used to separate observed sign distribution from reconstructed linguistic value.
